description:
SinkWatch | Seeing the Ground Move from Space
I'm Muhammad Asif, a recent Computer Science graduate, AI engineer and Research Assistant at a space tech Lab , working on remote sensing. Cities worldwide are sinking as groundwater is overpumped. SinkWatch uses NASA's new NISAR L-band radar to map which neighbourhoods are sinking, how fast, and who is at risk. From Quetta to Jakarta and Mexico City: satellite insight before the cracks appear. Built solo from Pakistan.
summary: Cities around the world are sinking as groundwater is pumped faster than it refills: Jakarta, Tehran, Mexico City and Quetta among them. The damage (cracked buildings, broken pipes, worse flooding) usually goes unnoticed until it is too late. SinkWatch is an interactive web app that turns free NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar data into a map anyone can read: how fast the ground is sinking, which neighbourhoods are affected, and how many people live there. Tested first on Quetta, Pakistan, it found parts of the valley sinking up to about 16 cm per year, with nearly 270,000 people living where the ground sinks faster than 5 cm per year. The same pipeline works for any city NISAR passes over, so planners can act before the cracks appear.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SinkWatch shows where a city is sinking, how fast, and who lives there. Open the app and the map shows sinking ground in red. Move the cursor anywhere and a live readout shows the sinking speed, status and number of people nearby; click to pin a point and see elevation, a movement-over-time chart and a trend-confidence score. A time-lapse shows the sinking building up from June to October 2026. The Exposure tab counts people and area at each risk level, and "Analyze your data" lets anyone upload their own ground-motion map (GeoTIFF) and get the same analysis instantly. Light and dark mode, and a fullscreen dashboard, make it easy to present.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: nine consecutive NISAR L2 GUNW interferograms over Quetta (track 041 ascending, frame 017, 17 Jun - 15 Oct 2026), streamed directly from NASA's ASF DAAC, downloading only a few MB of the 20.8 GB.

2. Cleaning: subtracted NISAR's ionosphere phase screen, then removed atmospheric and terrain-linked errors by fitting each pair against the Copernicus GLO-30 elevation model, using only data outside an 8 km circle around the city so the real sinking is never removed.

3. Measuring: stacked the nine pairs, converted line-of-sight motion to vertical, and estimated the yearly sinking rate for every 80 m pixel, with an R² trend-confidence score so noisy points are flagged.

4. Focus: limited statistics to the soft valley floor (elevation < 1,900 m, slope < 5°), where groundwater subsidence happens.

5. Impact: overlaid WorldPop 2020 population to count people living on sinking ground.

6. App: Python (Streamlit, Folium/Leaflet, Plotly), live online.

RESULTS (QUETTA, PROVISIONAL DATA)

- City centre: about 9 cm/yr; fastest 1% of the valley: about 16.6 cm/yr

- About 99 km² sinking faster than 5 cm/yr, about 35 km² faster than 10 cm/yr

- About 268,500 people living on ground sinking faster than 5 cm/yr; about 119,000 faster than 10 cm/yr

- Hotspot location and rates are consistent with published Sentinel-1 InSAR and GPS studies of the Quetta Valley (3.2 to 16 cm/yr)

IMPACT

- Protect neighbourhoods: see which streets and buildings to inspect first

- Manage groundwater: find where pumping is making the city sink

- Early warning: catch fast sinking before floods and damage

- Free and scalable: no field surveys, works for any city NISAR covers every 12 days

WHAT IS NEW

SinkWatch uses NISAR's first public L-band data, turns a complex radar product into a tool a city engineer, planner or citizen can use in a browser, and links ground motion directly to the people living on it.

LIMITATIONS

120 days of provisional data; one viewing direction (vertical motion assumed); some residual atmosphere away from the valley. Exposure shows who lives on sinking ground, not building damage. Results will sharpen as NISAR collects more passes.

NEXT STEPS

Jakarta, Tehran and Mexico City through the same pipeline; then any city on Earth processed automatically from the latest NISAR pass; then alerts when a neighbourhood starts sinking faster.

Built solo by Muhammad Asif, Pakistan.
